subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF "WOODSIDE" AS NATIONAL PARK

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF "WOODSIDE" AS NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
I have a short announcement to make regarding Woodside, the boyhood home of the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
The Woodside property includes the old residence and about eleven acres of wooded land in Kitchener, Ontario. Plans to restore the site were made by a group of interested citizens in 1942. It was not until 1950, however, that it was possible to bring these plans to fruition. In that year the Mackenzie King Woodside trust was established as a nonprofit, non-political corporation with the purpose of restoring Woodside. Contributions were received by the trust from Canadians in many walks of life, and the trust has since carried out the physical restoration of the site at a cost of some $90,000.
Shortly after the work was started the directors of the trust approached the federal government with the suggestion that when restoration was completed Woodside be made a national historic park. This proposal was referred to the historic sites and monuments board of Canada. The board, after investigation, declared Woodside to be a site of national historic importance and recommended that it be taken over and maintained as a national historic park. The recommendation of the board was made in May, 1952. The restoration having been completed, it has now been decided to accept the offer of the trust and to take over the site as a national historic park as of April 1, 1954.

Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house in regard to negotiations with Japan for the exchange of most-favoured-nation trade treatment. As hon. members are aware, these discussions have sought a treaty which would be mutually beneficial to both countries. An agreement on commerce between Japan and Canada was signed this morning by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself and by the ambassador of Japan to Canada.
The Canadian government welcomes the signing today of the trade agreement with Japan which, when it is ratified and comes into force, should contribute to the prosperity and good trading relations of both countries. Japan is a great trading nation and last year was Canada's third best customer. The importance of the agreement, however, goes beyond commercial considerations, for the agreement should also contribute to stable and friendly relations between the two countries and to the peace and security and progress of the Pacific area. If the house so wishes, I shall table the agreement now and outline its principal provisions.
Under the terms of this agreement Canada and Japan will exchange unconditional mostfavoured-nation trade treatment. The agreement also provides that neither country will impose or maintain restrictions or prohibitions affecting its trade with the other country unless similar measures are applied equally to all third countries. Similarly, in the allocation of foreign exchange and in the administration of foreign exchange restrictions affecting trade, each country will accord unconditional most-favoured-nation treatment.
In a supplementary exchange of notes which is appended to the agreement Canada reserves the right to establish special values for duty on any imports entering Canada in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers of like or directly competitive products. In the event of such special values being applied, and in

Trade Agreement with Japan determining the level at which such values should be applied, Canada will take into account the prices of like or directly competitive products imported from other countries.
Under the agreement either country may temporarily impose discriminatory import and exchange restrictions, if such restrictions are required on balance of payments grounds. However, such restrictions must not discriminate between Canada and other dollar countries or other countries with convertible currencies. The government of Japan has also undertaken, subject to certain agreed exceptions, to accord Canada unconditional nondiscriminatory treament in relation to any other country with respect to import and exchange controls on the following nine commodities: wheat, barley, woodpulp, flaxseed, primary copper, lead in pigs, zinc spelter, synthetic resins and milk powder.
The agreement also provides for non-discrimination in state trading practices. Both countries undertake to conform to internationally accepted fair trade practices, particularly in matters pertaining to trade marks, marks of origin and rights under patents. They also undertake to co-operate in the prevention of any practices which might prejudicially affect their mutual trade and to accord sympathetic consideration to any representations that the other country may make.
The two countries have agreed that the provisions of this agreement continue to be applicable in the event that the general agreement on tariffs and trade is applied between Canada and Japan.
As I have indicated, this agreement will enter into force on its ratification by both countries. A resolution for approval of ratification will be introduced in the house as soon as possible.

On what value is our paper money presently based?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Bank of Canada notes are legal tender in fulfilment of any contracts made in terms of Canadian money. The Bank of Canada Act provides that these notes shall be redeemable in gold, in the form of bars. It also provides that the bank shall maintain a gold reserve equal to at least 25 per cent of its note and deposit liabilities and may in addition keep a reserve in certain kinds of foreign exchange. At present, the operation of these provisions is suspended, and Canada's official reserves of gold and foreign exchange are centralized in the exchange fund.
The total of Canada's official holdings of gold and United States dollars is published monthly, and at the end of February comprised $1,007-8 million of gold, and $845-7 million of United States dollars which are convertible into gold. Both the foregoing amounts are expressed in terms of United States dollars. At the end of February the Bank of Canada's note and deposit liabilities amounted to 1,506 and 837 million Canadian dollars respectively.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. I must apologize for having given him such short notice. In view of the recent conviction of a Canadian soldier reported to have the mental age of ten, can the minister tell the house whether the Department of National Defence takes any precautions to prevent mental defectives from enlisting in the services? Is there not something better that Canada can do for these unfortunate people?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PRECAUTIONS TO PREVENT ENLISTMENT OF MENTAL DEFECTIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) having just returned after several days absence, and as I received notice of the hon. member's question just before entering the house, perhaps I might be permitted to deal with it.
I would say in the first place that each of the services has established through a set of mental and physical tests a general system of examination of recruits to give effect to a policy of enrolling the right type of service personnel. Whatever those standards may be, I can assure my hon. friend that they are such that those who pass them must be far beyond the mental age of ten. The tests are carefully worked out and have resulted extremely well in most cases. Of course there will always be borderline cases wherever the line is drawn. Some borderline cases turn out very well, and some not so well. This is one of the unfortunate ones.
I would like to add that I believe the average type of Canadian citizen enrolled in the services, whether he has served in Korea, in Europe or here in Canada, has achieved excellent results and has given an excellent account of himself.
As to the second question, my reply would be that I think most hon. members and the public generally agree that the standard of assistance accorded to our unfortunate citizens here in Canada is probably higher than in any other country of the world.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate which is now before this house, it is not my intention to be unduly repetitious nor to speak upon any of the subjects which have been discussed here during these past few days. It has been a lengthy debate but, in my opinion, it has been a most useful and worth-while one. We have heard discussion and statements from the government and from members of the opposition on such matters as the Berlin conference, the projected Geneva conference, and arms to Pakistan; arguments for and against the recognition of Red China; and academic discussions on communism and anti-communism. All of these things are of the utmost importance and the discussion was worth while. However, Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at all on all of those matters, important as they are. I do not profess to be an expert on foreign affairs and so I shall leave all those discussions to those who are experts or who profess to be. There is, however, one phase that comes under this debate upon which I feel impelled to speak. In doing so, I admit I am not doing it because I am a scientist; I am not. I am doing it because of the crucial and critical matters that have been drawn to the attention of the peoples of the world, in particular in the last few weeks. I refer to the matter of the hydrogen bomb.

It has been intimated clearly upon more than one occasion by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) that he intends to speak and that he looks forward with anticipation to the remarks which he will make at the close of this debate. I fully realize that he will undoubtedly be commenting upon many of the things that have been said by the various speakers during the past few days and will undoubtedly be answering a number of the questions that have been hurled at him. But my purpose in rising at this time is to tell the Secretary of State for External Affairs that I think he would be seriously derelict in his duty or in his responsibility if he were not able, when he speaks, to take the House of Commons and the people of Canada into his confidence and give all the information possible as to the situation with regard to the hydrogen bomb; the policies as far as he knows them that are now in existence involving the experimentation in the use of that bomb; and, of more importance, the proposals which the minister may have or, I think I will say, should have as to the stand which Canada should take in this critical period of our history.
There are undoubtedly millions of people in this world who believe in the statement that a deity created the world in six days and rested on the seventh. There are undoubtedly many more millions who do not take that view but who accept the view of scientists that through the process of evolution over millions of years the world as we know it came to its present form. I am not going into any academic discussion of how the world came into being. But the fact is this. Over untold millions of years there has been in existence this world, but we are now in the position, in the year 1954, where all the evidence makes it completely conclusive that, unless there is some sanity in the parliaments of the world and unless we arrive at sanity between the nations of the world, man in his stupidity can in the matter of minutes or hours definitely destroy mankind and perhaps the world itself.
Admittedly we are a small nation but we are an important one. In my humble opinion this house could do well by spending a little bit more time to see whether it would not be possible for us to arrive at policies and conclusions whereby the Secretary of State for External Affairs or perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) could give a militant, sane and dynamic lead to the other leaders throughout the world as to what should be done in view of the situation as it is understood by the people since the explosion of the first hydrogen bomb on March 1. It is no exaggeration to state that if we have such people who can release the

spark, another war might start. It was only the spark of the shooting of one man of royalty that, officially at least, started the first world war. It was the lunacy of one man in Germany, with his dreams of power, that caused the actions that set off the spark which started the second world war. Who knows what may start the third? If it does start, the evidence is conclusive that it means the end of mankind.
We have the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs before the Ottawa Catholic youth organization, as reported in the press only a few days ago:
If the nations of the world engage in a third world war, civilization would be destroyed, . . .
That is our own Secretary of State for External Affairs. In this morning's Globe and Mail we find a statement attributed to one who should know. I refer to Defence Secretary Charles E. Wilson of the United States. Here is what he has to say, as reported in the paper:
Defence Secretary Charles E. Wilson said today the unbelievable power unleashed in test H-bomb explosions this month dwarfed the atomic bomb just as the A-bomb dwarfed TNT bombs of the second world war.
Mr. Holifield, a member of the United States congress and a member of the congressional atomic energy committee, who saw the March 1 explosion, has this to say, as reported in the same paper:
Holifield, who saw the effects of the titanic March 1 hydrogen explosion, told the house, however, that "civil defence against atomic-hydrogen attack is a delusion . . . mass extermination of millions in any or all nations can occur during a week end."
And further:
Holifield said complete military defence against supersonic planes or missiles with atomic-hydrogen warheads is impossible and non-existent.
Mr. Wilson said further:
Wilson was asked at a news conference whether the U.S. intends to use the H-bomb if it is involved in another war. He replied: "Don't you think it would be foolish to spend billions unless you are prepared to use them under some circumstances?"
I think you will understand, Mr. Speaker, the reason why I feel so intensely about this matter. Here we have statements by leaders of the North American continent, including our own Secretary of State for External Affairs, the defence secretary of the United States and a member of the congress of the United States who saw that explosion on March 1. They all agreed that the result of the destructive power of the hydrogen bomb means the end of mankind, and they also stated that there is no military or civil defence whatsoever against the power of the hydrogen bomb.
External Affairs
That is why I suggest that this matter should be discussed and a lead given to us and, I hope, to the world, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). This was brought very forcibly to my attention in an excellent editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Daily Sun on March 27. With your permission, sir, I would like to quote part of that editorial. It states:
Churchill contemplating the effects of H-bombing nearly weeps in public. Eisenhower, stupefied by news of the scientists' surprise, implies he is stunned by bombing possibilities. All common men everywhere, probably even in Russia, are aghast and voice their dread. Yet no move is made to deal with the H-bomb threat. We believe common men hold their safety and desire to live at peace in their own hands. We believe they can make themselves heard through their governments and elected representatives. Convinced that now is the time for positive action, we suggest the cabinet at Ottawa, through Prime Minister St. Laurent, call for a world conference using the machinery of the United Nations headquarters at New York.
We suggest that he lose no time in asking for this conference. In many countries Canada has ambassadors. Let them pass on the call.
The conference should be summoned in a spirit of absolute objectivity. There must be no ideological fences erected. It must be bombs and nothing but the bombs.
The time for form and ceremony is past and the hour demands immediate action by some one man who does not fear to risk position, or the condescending smiles of statesmen higher in the councils of the world.
I believe that is an excellent editorial, Mr. Speaker. I think it is a call to members of this house to do a little soul searching and see if we cannot adopt a responsible attitude at this session, in this house, at this time and get away from an academic discussion of communism, anti-communism, the recognition of China, or what happened at the Berlin conference, and lay down a program in clear terms calling now for the rule of sanity among the leaders of the nations of this world. The only place I know where such can be directed is through the medium of the United Nations.
A few years ago we might have called that epoch the age of TNT. That gave way to the age of the atom, but already the atom has given way to the hydrogen bomb. I have been trying to find out something about the atomic and hydrogen bomb and I came across what I believe is a magnificent book which can be understood by laymen. It is entitled, "Scientific American Reader". Upon reading that book I learned that there are two differences between the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb. The atomic bomb and indeed the entire atomic energy enterprise rests ultimately on the basic reaction following the splitting of uranium 235. On the other hand, the hydrogen bomb is not based on fission, it is based on fusion. There is

External Affairs
another major difference. Atomic energy can be used not only for destruction but also for construction and for power. If this scientific journal is correct, the hydrogen bomb can never be used, or at least cannot now be used, for constructive purposes. It can only be used in the sense of destruction.
I would like to quote one paragraph from an article in this book written by that great North American physicist Louis N. Ridenour. This is what he says:
. . . while fission can be controlled in an orderlyway to produce useful power in a reactor, the fusion reaction offers no prospect at the present time of any use except in terms of an explosion. We cannot find in the development of the fusion bomb any such peacetime values as are inherent in the development of nuclear fission. Except where the uses of peace demand the detonation of an explosive equivalent to, say, a million tons of TNT, there is no use for a fusion reaction. Thus when we discuss the "hydrogen bomb" we are clearly speaking of a weapon, and a weapon only.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that leads me to what I may call a more practical point. Can we have some understanding as to what is taking place in the Pacific? May I say that I am not directing any criticism against the United States alone, but I believe we have got to direct our thinking toward the United States and the U.S.S.R., both of whom have experimented in exploding a hydrogen bomb.
I was amazed to read in today's issue of the New York Times that it is only in the last six months that the United States has caught up with the technology of the U.S.S.R. in the explosion of the hydrogen bomb. This is not a matter which concerns the U.S.S.R. and the United States only. It is a matter which concerns the world. It definitely concerns us in the Dominion of Canada, particularly as far as the explosions in the Pacific are concerned.
I would like to know by what authority and by what power the United States obtains rule over a part of the Pacific ocean in regard to current hydrogen experiments which may affect the people of the Dominion of Canada. President Eisenhower himself admitted that the scientists have been amazed. They have moved into the realm of the unknown, a realm in which I believe they have no business. Indeed, they are entering into the realm of the supernatural. They were amazed by the explosion on March 1, and they have already stated that for the explosion scheduled for April they will extend the official danger area by 20 times, and it is only recently that some of the things which have occurred have come to light.
If we can accept the press reports, what do we find? We find that there was radioactive ash over 71 miles from the point of the

explosion, and there are a number of Japanese sailors who are living proof of that. We also find that the explosion was such that United States marines 225 miles away saw the explosion. When you consider the perimeter of the earth it will be evident that, to see an explosion 225 miles away, the effects of that explosion would have to go far up into the heavens. We also learned that when United States scientists made certain tests they found the ocean was radioactive 800 miles away from the point of the explosion.
That was their smallest bomb. Now, Mr. Speaker, where can this lead to and why am I as a Canadian so interested? I am interested not only from the viewpoint of preventing war and saving mankind and civilization, but also from the viewpoint of the people of Canada. Already we have heard several hon. members ask questions in this house about the radioactive snow in Saskatchewan and in Winnipeg, Manitoba. We have heard it said:	Yes, it was radioactive but not
dangerous. It may not have been dangerous with that first explosion but there it is over 5,000 miles from the point of explosion. How do we know that it will not be dangerous to the people of this country and other countries when the larger bomb goes off? We have also got to recognize that so far as the United States is concerned these explosions take place in the Pacific ocean. I have actually met people who have the fallacious view that is the place to explode such bombs because there the danger disseminates. It diffuses, and within miles it is gone. Oceanography proves that is a fallacy. It is not like throwing a pebble into a little pool where the concentric circles gradually diminish and disappear.
Oceanography proves that the ocean is different because as you have highways across Canada, as you have channels of air in the atmosphere above us, so you have currents and actual rivers in the ocean cutting through narrow sections of the entire ocean. Sometimes they are only a few miles wide and sometimes several hundred miles wide, but whether in the upper level of the ocean or in what has been referred to as the sunless sea, the bottom section of the ocean, there are these channels of currents and rivers. Some of these channels and currents that start in the mid-Pacific thousands of miles from the Canadian coast reach the shore of the province of British Columbia. It is already admitted that the ocean was found to be radioactive 800 miles from the small explosion. What will happen with the larger explosion when we have these currents that touch the Canadian coast?

You may say that some of these things are problematical. I admit that they are, but in view of what we have read and heard in the past few,weeks there are mighty serious questions that should be asked and not only asked but answered. The minister should tell us as far as he can about what information he has gained from consultation with the United States and also through the United Nations with respect to the position of the U.S.S.R. I say that it is a heinous thing that the world's two most powerful nations, the U.S.S.R. and the United States, should take into their own hands the power of a physical god on earth by their experimentation with and probable use of the hydrogen bomb.
I speak as an individual. We are only a small nation but we should make our voice heard. With the stature and status that Canada has it can give a lead. At least the words of the minister would be noted in the press and in the consultative bodies of the world if he would come out with a definite statement and challenge at this time in the rostrum of 15 million people, the House of Commons of Canada.
That is the practical side of the question. There is also the moral aspect, and I should like to read certain remarks of the physicist I quoted a few moments ago beause they put the situation in far better words than I could choose. I think they drive home the point exceptionally well. He said:
I believe the most important question is the moral one: can we who have always insisted on morality and human decency between nations as well as inside our own country, introduce this weapon of total annihilation into the world? . . . What would an all-out war fought with hydrogen bombs mean? It would mean the obliteration of all large cities and probably of many smaller ones, and the killing of most of their inhabitants. After such a war, nothing that resembled present civilization would remain. The fight for mere survival would dominate everything. The destruction of the cities might set technology back a hundred years or more. In a generation even the knowledge of technology and science might disappear, because there would be no opportunity to practise them. Indeed it is likely that technology and science, having brought such utter misery upon man, would be suspected as works of the devil, and that a new dark age would begin on earth.
I think these words are true. I think they point up in concise form the statements that have been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he says that a third world war will mean the destruction of civilization. Statements have been made throughout the world that another war will mean the end of mankind. The secretary of war of the United States has stated that they are not producing these bombs for fun, that they hope they will be a
External Affairs
deterrent but that if a spark starts a war then under certain circumstances this weapon will be used which it is admitted will destroy mankind and the nations of the world.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is time for a little common-sense thinking. I ask, and as a matter of fact I go further and plead with the minister, who, I know, has a great sense of responsibility and a great sense of justice, to take under advisement the giving of a lead at this time to the world, the issuing of a challenge to his colleagues in the United Nations to get down to the matter and discuss nothing else but bombs.

Mr. Speaker, having returned only yesterday from Pakistan and India I have not had the privilege of hearing this debate but I have heard enough to realize that further contributions may not be gratefully received. Nevertheless, I feel that this may be the only opportunity I shall have to make a very brief report on a conference which I think has some bearing on the subject matter of this debate. My journey took the same route as that of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), not by design, as was suggested by some, but because my purpose was to attend a conference in Lahore and it happened to take place shortly after his visit there.
I should like, first of all, to bear witness to the impression I got of his visit three weeks after he had been there, and while, in both Pakistan and India, the memory was fresh. The greatest respect was paid to our Prime Minister, and the relationships between those two countries and Canada were undoubtedly improved by that very gracious visit.
May I make another acknowledgment which my friend the minister may appreciate, namely that I and others who were on this mission received the greatest co-operation and assistance from our Canadian representatives in the cities where we needed their help. This began in London and was continued in New Delhi, the capital of India, and Karachi, the capital of Pakistan, where we were cordially aided and assisted in our unofficial purposes.
The conference, Mr. Speaker, was an entirely unofficial conference. It was a conference amongst the members of the commonwealth, a discussion meeting for the purpose of exchanging ideas and understanding each other's point of view, thus improving relationships. All members of the commonwealth were represented, that is the five older members of the commonwealth, of British origin, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand, and in addition the three new Asiatic members of the commonwealth. I take the opportunity of saying a word today just to explain my impression of the viewpoint of those three associates of ours in the commonwealth who are Asiatic countries.
The conference was held at Lahore, which is the capital city of Punjab, one of the provinces which constitute Pakistan. Pakistan, India and Ceylon are the three Asiatic members of the commonwealth. I think it was
fMr. Winch.]
fortunate that the Institute of International Affairs, which sponsors these conferences every five years, chose Pakistan as the scene of this conference. The conference brought together a very strong representative delegation from each of the countries of the commonwealth. The United Kingdom delegation, by way of illustration, had four members of the House of Commons, three of whom were former ministers, including a former chancellor of the exchequer, as well as a former marshal of the air force as a military adviser. Then, there were a number of academic people who make international studies their particular interest. Attached to them were members of three dependencies, two very fine citizens from the new federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, now approaching the point where they may become full members of the commonwealth.
There was an African lawyer of great ability from the West Indies who gave an excellent account of himself and of the experiment in self-government in the British West Indies, a very encouraging thing. Then, there was a minister from the Federation of Malaya, which is under a tutelage system, looking towards full self-government. From Canada we had a delegation of eight; from South Africa there were five or six representing different viewpoints; and there were delegates from Australia, New Zealand and so on. Pakistan was represented by a strong group of thirteen, two university presidents, and the Speaker of the Punjab legislature was chairman of their delegation. I believe he attended here the year before last when the commonwealth parliamentary association met in Ottawa. India had a large delegation.
Our discussions in that ancient city of Lahore, which was the capital of the Mogul empire at one time and later the scene of British administration of that great province, occupied twelve days. We ranged from the strategical and political relationship of the members of the commonwealth through racial and other matters which were of common interest. When I say that Canada was held in high esteem, I believe one reason is that we have never in our history been subjected to the charge of colonialism or imperialism and we have never had any serious race problems. These two elements of human relationships are always present in the minds of eastern people, and one has to think of them throughout any discussion of commonwealth relations. Canada is free from any difficulty on that score.
My impression of our Asiatic friends in the commonwealth was that their first interest, as countries having recently achieved their independence, was the economic development

of their own country. They appreciate their underdeveloped state. They appreciate that they lag behind other countries of the commonwealth, and their main concern is for an era of peace in which they can bring about the developments which will raise the standard of living in their own country.
The second feature that colours all their thinking is that common Asiatic view that the European has no right or place in dominating the people of Asia. I found, to my surprise, that concern of the Asiatic peoples even affected their view towards NATO. We regard NATO as an alliance for defensive purposes only and related to defence in western Europe, but they were so concerned about the presence in any Asiatic country of western Europeans that the presence of France in Indo-China was of more concern to them than the threat of communism. They felt that in some way NATO might be assisting France to maintain and carry on that conflict in Indo-China, which to them was very largely an imperialist struggle between a nationalist movement on the one hand and a western dominating power on the other.
I feel that our discussions did something to offset that view of the western defensive arrangement and the alliances involved. I have raised the question here because in any of our external relationships which involve commonwealth countries it is necessary to bear in mind that the Asiatic members of our group do feel more strongly about the subjugation of people in Asia, a subjugation which they have recently broken, than they do about the threat of communism. It will be a matter of education over a period of time to change that viewpoint, and it varies, of course, amongst the three countries concerned.
I found that Pakistan was very cordially concerned with the problems of the West, much more interested than India whose delegation reiterated the neutrality policies of Mr. Nehru and, with difficulty, would concede that they were in any need of following any other course. Now, that was the main impression of the conference that I wanted to mention. I mention this view of our Asiatic friends because I feel that their importance in the world today is such that it is to our interest, not only because they are members of the commonwealth but in the broader view of understanding of what moves them in this field of external affairs.
India, as you know, is a country of 340 million people. I suppose that is the greatest part of the population of the commonwealth. From this distance we may regard Pakistan as a small country, but with 30 million people in its western part and 43 million in the
External Affairs
eastern half, a total of 73 million, it places seventh among the nations of the world. They claim to be fifth, but I think Indonesia and Germany have to be counted in there. Ceylon is not an inconsiderable country, but is an island and is, I think, less concerned about current world affairs than the other two. The conference I believe brought to these two big Asiatic partners of ours some idea of the way the western countries feel about and look at the problem of communism. While India was not prepared to align herself positively with either the West or the East, but was content to keep to a middle position, Pakistan's recent moves-her treaty with Turkey and her acceptance of American military aid, and the views we heard expressed at this conference-would definitely indicate that she is to be counted as one of the western group.
As I say, the importance of these countries lies partly in their population and partly in the role they have to play in the future. We, as members of a group which have nothing to bind us together other than good will, can play a very useful part in retaining the confidence, good will and interest which exists in those countries today.
They value particularly the common parliamentary experience which has been their inheritance from British rule. They carry on their business in English. In fact, I think it would be impossible in Pakistan to conduct government without the use of English. And even in India it was freely expressed that although English was the language of their former rulers, it was nevertheless a great language in the world and had the additional advantage to them of being a common means of communication within the country as well as a means of communication in all their external relationships. I dare say that despite the nationalistic moves to promote Urdu and Hindi as the respective languages for the two countries, English will be the common means of communication of those governments and will be a common bond between those countries and the rest of the commonwealth.
The conference played some significant part, I suggest, in improving the understanding which is so essential. After all, understanding is the cement which makes these relationships grow and improve. I would close by making reference to Sir Edward Grey's remark, made in a different context, that nothing better promotes understanding than a consciousness of being understood.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess that on a number of occasions since coming to this house I have been tempted to think that a great deal of time has been spent on very small matters.

External Affairs
However, when we entered upon this particular debate, and as it has continued, it has been my conviction that we are now dealing with a phase of our deliberations that is of paramount importance.
I have been taught that men's relationships in life are of paramount concern. Those relationships perhaps can be summed up under three categories, the first of which is man's relationship to God. I feel that that is basic; that is the foundation.
The second is our relationship to our fellow man; and that is of tremendous importance.
The third is our relationship to things, or to the material world around us. It seems to me that we have been dealing with the most difficult of those three, namely our relationship with our fellow man. As I have been considering this matter and listening to the debates a verse from Scripture has come to my mind repeatedly. I shall not preach a sermon, although I am almost convinced that one would not be altogether out of order in doing so-for instance Winch versus the Bible, or something to that effect. But the verse is this:
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
I think that verse should be kept in mind; it is a splendid exhortation. I think that not only in our individual relationships but in our relationships with the various nations of the world we should keep in mind that exhortation from the book of Romans. Humanity being what it is, frictions are bound to arise. But so far as possible I think we must accept the responsibility for removing those causes of friction and cultivating friendships among all men. We must strive with other nations for the establishment of good will among all the peoples of the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to come to the matter which prompted me to enter this debate- and I shall not take very long this afternoon -I should like to speak of my own attitude and that of the group to which I belong toward this great question of peace. This has always been a great and wonderful theme. It has been something that men have sought after and nations have coveted. From one viewpoint alone, the moral viewpoint, we ought to search and explore every avenue whereby peace can be secured.
Now when we consider, as we have been considering the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb, and its effects and possibilities, the importance of this theme is further enhanced. Before I came here for the opening of the session last fall a delegation of about twenty men and women called upon me and asked me one question:	What is

your attitude toward peace? I was very happy to be able to tell them that I thought I was just as much in favour of peace as they were. I was just as anxious to see peace established and maintained as they were. And certainly that is still my attitude -and because of the fact that I suppose most of our families have suffered the results of war. I have no doubt that practically all our families have paid some price in wars that have been fought in the past.
Therefore my heart cries out for peace in the world; my prayer is for peace. And I know that other members in this group as well as other members in the House of Commons desire those same conditions of peace.
Following my maiden speech I had a letter from one of my constituents in which very kindly he referred to the remarks I had made, but said, "I deplore the fact that you did not raise your voice for the cause of peace." I replied of course and told him he had misread my speech, and gave him the part that dealt especially with this particular matter.
However, as we think of it today, as I have said, with the tremendous possibilities of war and the potential forces that are placed at man's disposal, we all desire in some way or other to find peace established in this world of ours. I am now speaking for the Social Credit group when I say we urge that every effort be made to resolve the differences between those behind the iron curtain and the free nations of the world. Every possible endeavour should be made in order to accomplish that end. No one in this group wants war. We do not desire just the cessation of hostilities; we desire that a true and lasting peace shall be established on earth.
We deplore aggression. We join with those who advocate collective action by the United Nations to stop acts of aggression, and we take the position that Canada should not and must not be a party to aggression in any sense. However, I think we must be realistic and realize that the world is in great danger of aggressive acts and intentions by other nations, and no one knows when or where they may create incidents- I say "they may create incidents"-which could lead to war. And should that happen -and we sincerely hope and pray that it may not-what is our stand going to be?
I am sure that every group in this house, and perhaps I should say all members with the exception of some hon. members in the group to my right, would take the view that the free nations of the world must not be let down, nor can we let our freedom and all that we hold dear be lost by default.

I think I should call attention to the statement made by the leader of our party in the speech that he delivered on January 29 in the debate on external affairs. These are the words, as found at page 1611 of Hansard:
My organization and I are committed to strive for international peace and security. We believe that Canada and all other nations should have been striving over the years with all their might to find out what are the real sources of war, and to remove those just as quickly as possible.
We should have been doing everything in our power to remove industrial rivalry among the nations, to establish an equitable distribution of the goods and services this world can produce, and to have them distributed in all nations that are willing to co-operate. We believe that perhaps the greatest single factor leading to International conflict has been the lack of such equitable distribution of the goods and services that were produced. We are unalterably of the opinion that the establishment of sound international trade policies, such as those we have outlined on many occasions, is the best assurance of international peace and security.
At the same time we recognize only too well that there is over the whole face of the world today a conflict of ideologies that is a constant threat to peace and national security. When we realize that this conflict is going on, then we also must be realistic in recognizing the necessity of organizations such as NATO and the European defence community and that sort of thing. We recognize also the necessity of organizing our own national economy so as to provide good opportunities for economic security for all of our people, along with freedom, so we can help them to be happy and contented in their lot and save them in the struggle that is going on for men's minds.
We hear much about peace and the opportunities for peace. We hon. members are getting letters almost every day from some peace organization. Because we speak sometimes with vigour, because we advocate all-out vigilance, some of us are often understood to be belligerent. I hope there will be an intelligent differentiation between the two, as certainly there is a difference. To be vigilant is not to be belligerent. Vigilance is all we want.
Then he went on to say-and I just quote a short statement:
Speaking of peace may I say that to us, except life itself and liberty there is probably nothing that we cherish as much as peace.
I wanted to place that on record, Mr. Speaker, because it states in a very definite and positive manner the policy of this particular group, and this afternoon I subscribe to that statement. My hope and my prayer is that in every way possible our leaders, this government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will exercise the influence that they have in the councils of the nations to bring about a true and a lasting peace.

speechtext:
During the course of this debate we have heard a great many comments about the hydrogen bomb. The hydrogen bomb is not of itself any problem, of course. It is merely a mechanical contrivance devised by man, and there would be no problem of the hydrogen bomb except
External Affairs
for two forces that are operating against each other in the world today. We have always had those two forces. One is a reasonable and logical force, and the other is an emotional one. They have been operating against each other all through history. You have a good example of that today. The emotional one is nationalism and the logical one is the desire of the countries of the world today to try to get together in some kind of national cooperation such as the United Nations and on a smaller scale such as NATO, and so on.
Nationalism has always been a factor. That is very true, but today it has become more prominent because of the political emergence of the Asiatic countries, particularly those of southeast Asia, and the Middle Eastern countries. These countries, for varying periods of time, have been under the domination of many of the western countries, and they have recently emerged as individual entities. Thus the emotional question of nationalism has made itself very prominent indeed today.
What is this thing called "nationalism"? You see the word used a lot, and I think we ought to make some attempt to define what it might be. A very simple definition, which I can assure you is my own, and no one else's, and of course open to criticism, is that nationalism is the determination of a group of individuals to assert themselves. To go on from there, I say "a group of individuals", and you may ask:	Can we narrow it down
even more? Well, since individuals tend to identify themselves with groups of people, the emotional reasoning can be referred back to the individual. I think this can be best exemplified by a little story I once heard. It was during Queen Victoria's diamond jubilee, when all the princes from India and from other parts of the empire at that time were travelling through the streets of London. A little cockney down on the corner poked his neighbour as one particularly gorgeous Indian prince was going by all bejewelled and on a bejewelled elephant and said: "Look, we owns him." I think that illustrates fairly well how this business of the individual identifying himself with a group comes about, and it is very important.
We have now got down to individuals, and I am trying to simplify this very complex problem. What drives an individual to want to assert himself?
In the last century a prominent Viennese gentleman called Sigmund Freud, with whose name I think everybody is familiar, started the study of what motivated human beings. I think by and large psychologists, people who study the reasons for human behaviour, would generally agree even yet that probably the basic reason for human beings desiring to assert themselves is probably related

External Affairs
back to-and I hesitate to use this word in the house-the sex drive. In any event, the human desire to assert one's self really does go back to some emotional rather than logical drive. There are various ways that can aggravate or increase this desire to assert one's self. In some cases it is just like Topsy in "Uncle Tom's Cabin", just growing up, just being adolescent; you want to show off to your elders a little bit and to make them think that you really are important and that you do know something.
But on the other hand certain things such as suppression and frustration and so on can also make people want to assert themselves. You can now apply these things to groups; I mean groups of people who have been suppressed or frustrated in their national desires. That can aggravate their nationalism or their desire to assert themselves. Other things can enter into it, such as just growing up as in the case of a new country, such as the new Asiatic countries. Even in Canada, for example, we are touchy about little things such as a national flag and the desire that Americans should not think that the King or the Queen actually rule us and that we do not rule ourselves. We are very touchy on little things like that. Nationalism can take various forms.
First of all, let us see about the individual. There are two forms, namely the active and the passive. The passive form of nationalism is of course usually very constructive. Let us look at the individual who wants to assert himself in a constructive way. He may become a great artist or a great scientist or something like that and do something constructive. This again applies to a group of people or individuals such as a country. Ancient Egypt is a good example. Egypt did a lot to contribute to the arts of peace and they were never particularly prominent in war. Ancient Greece in its early days was more noted for the arts of peace than for the arts of war and so on. These are examples of constructive nationalism.
In the more active aspect as far as individuals are concerned, you have the town bully who wants to force his will on somebody else and you have religious fanatics who are determined to force their religious views down somebody else's throat. Referring again to groups of people, you have nations who desire to assert themselves by forcing their national culture upon everyone else. Sometimes people refer to the United States as wishing to do that, thinking that they have the best way of life and wanting to make sure that everybody else has it. In the Middle Ages the Mohammedans and the Turks had that point of view. They tried to

force the Islamic cultures on a large part of Europe. Certain nations have strong national political views, like Russia, and desire to force communism on the rest of the world.
I think I have dealt long enough with nationalism in an abstract way and should get down to a consideration of just where does this affect Canada. As I have said, we have a little bit of nationalism in Canada; I refer to our touchiness about things such as the flag and so on.
I think Canada is in a particularly fortunate position in the world. We often hear about Canada being a linchpin between England and the United States and that we can interpret England to the United States and vice versa. I think Canada should continue to be this kind of linchpin, but I think we could very well be another linchpin in the same kind of world machine. I think we would make a very fine linchpin between the new Asiatic countries and the western world such as United States, Great Britain, France and so on. I think Canada is probably the best suited to do this of all the western countries.
The remarks that have just been made by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) who has just returned from the East, express that very well. Canada, like the new Asiatic countries, is a new country in a political sense. It is not, of course, in a cultural sense like the Asiatic countries. Their cultural history goes back centuries and even for thousands of years. But politically Asiatic countries like Pakistan, Indonesia, the Philippines and the Middle Eastern countries like Iraq, Iran and Egypt are all new countries politically. So is Canada. It is something we have in common.
Canada has never been in a position where we have attempted to dominate these countries in a political sense as Great Britain, France and the United States have done in the past or in the economic sense as I think the United States has often been falsely accused of doing nowadays. For those reasons the newer countries do not suspect the motives of Canada. More than that, we are too small, at least on a population basis, to attempt to force our will on those other countries and for that reason we are not suspect. More than that, for the last few years we have been very generous in giving gifts of food and mutual aid-I refer to such things as the Colombo plan and so on-to these Asiatic countries. I think they appreciate it, and they do not suspect our motives.
I have some knowledge of this matter in a personal way. There are a number of people from Pakistan living in the town in

which I live. They have been there for almost a year now, and they will be there a little bit longer, learning agricultural methods. I have talked to them on many occasions. These people like Canada a great deal. They have been completely accepted in the community. They have had a very good time here. They like this country. They realize that we are not in any way attempting to interfere in their domestic affairs, in their foreign affairs or anything else, and that we only have a genuine desire to help them. They realize that when we give something to those countries we are not asking any quid pro quo in exchange. For these reasons I think that Canada should try to become a new linchpin between the East and the West and act as an interpreter of the western viewpoint to the East. My colleague from Vancouver -Quadra (Mr. Green) suggested a little bit earlier that Canada should enter into some of these Pacific pacts and take an active part. I thoroughly agree with him. I think that such participation would assist us in becoming a linchpin.
Mr. Speaker, I hope these few .remarks will be of some help. Accordingly, I should just like to commend them to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are looking forward to hearing the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). In order to facilitate matters I am going to make my remarks as brief as possible. However, as the member for Regina City I feel that I have a duty to my constituents to place before this house some observations which I feel might be of some value to the minister and to the government, and to comment upon some of the remarks that have been made during the course of this debate.
I for one am not perturbed by the fact that this debate has gone on for a number of days. As a faithful reader of Hansard for quite some years before coming to this house I have always felt a little bit of alarm at the manner in which external affairs were treated in the house; I refer to the idea that external affairs were something for which we would just set aside a day for a debate and then, after disposing of it in that summary fashion, get on with the business of the house. I feel that this debate indicates keen interest in external affairs among members of this house; and I think that is a reflection of the keen interest in foreign affairs throughout the country.
After listening to some of the speeches made in the debate, I found that there are many that I thoroughly appreciate. As to a
External Affairs
number of the speeches made, while I did not appreciate all the contents or all the remarks in those speeches, nevertheless I felt that they made a distinct contribution to the debate. They were made in a very forthright manner. They were based on some degree of logic, unlike some of the speeches which departed almost entirely from any semblance to logic or historical fact. Consequently I want to deal with a number of matters that I think have been dealt with perhaps in an incorrect way in the house.
A great deal has been said during the course of this debate on the question of the recognition of the Peking government, and I believe part of the difficulty, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the public, particularly the public in the United States, has been sold the idea that there is something synonymous between the terms recognition and approval. Of course, feeling as we do about the Chinese government, if recognition did imply any degree of approval I am sure we would disapprove of such recognition. But the difficulty we find ourselves in today is that many people will not realize that recognition does not involve approval.
When we of the C.C.F. have from time to time recommended the recognition of the Chinese government we have had people call us "fellow travellers" and make uncomplimentary remarks, completely ignoring the fact that the recognition of the Peking government has been advocated by many Canadians in various walks of life and of various political parties. The point of view we have set forth is the point of view taken by the British Conservative government. It will be recalled that last evening the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) dealt with that very matter and pointed out that the British Conservative government under the leadership of the Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill today recognize the Peking government. If that government did not approve of the policy of recognition it would be a relatively simple matter for the British government to withdraw their recognition. But they have not done so. Therefore, if there is anything wrong about our advocacy of the recognition of the Peking government then the criticism directed against us must also be directed against the British government. Even in our own country it will be noted by those who follow the press that many leading newspapers all across Canada have come out in support of the recognition of the Peking government.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his statement on Thursday last he quoted from an editorial which was published in the Ottawa Journal on Friday, March 12.

External Affairs
The Prime Minister did not quote the editorial in its entirety, but I should like to draw the attention of the house to several paragraphs of that editorial which I believe are pertinent to the point under discussion. The Journal goes on to say:
No country can ever know with certainty whether the government possessed by some other country is the government its people want. And the fact is that Canada now recognizes any number of countries without being at all sure that their government is what their people want. There is Russia, and Czechoslovakia, and Poland, and Spain; possibly others.
What Canada does, and must be compelled to do, and what all other countries must be compelled to do sooner or later, just because it is the only sensible practicable way, is to recognize the government of the country which is in effective control -which exists in fact. That, of course, must apply to China. There in an ancient historic nation a revolutionary movement defeated the government of Chiang Kai-shek, drove its armies from the China mainland, set up a new regime. Can we in Canada say sensibly or realistically that this new regime cannot act for the Chinese people, that it is not what the Chinese people want, and that until we discover that it is what the Chinese people want, we cannot recognize it as China's government, exercising authority.
The next day the Ottawa Citizen said almost the very same thing, the thing that we of the C.C.F. group have been saying. The Citizen editorial of March 13, under the heading "Korean Criticism of Mr. St. Laurent" said:
"Korea Republic", a semi-official newspaper published in Seoul, has criticized Prime Minister St. Laurent's opinion that diplomatic recognition of communist China is ultimately inevitable. In its criticism, the newspaper has expressed a viewpoint common to the lunatic fringe of the anticommunist camp, which would deny all hope of a peaceful settlement of issues that contribute to world tension. Korea Republic suggests that anyone, however well meaning, is a "communist tool", if he advocates a course, on any specific issue, that has been approved by the communists; further that diplomatic recognition of the Peiping regime constitutes moral acceptance. On both counts, Korea Republic is surely in error.
Decisions in the non-communist world should not be based essentially on whether or not the communists would favour them, so much as on whether they would help establish a stable peace without weakening the West vis-d-vis Russia and China. If statesmen are to become "communist tools" whenever their views coincide with those of Moscow, the communists could control the West simply by advocating policies the reverse of those the Kremlin really desires. The Labour-Progressive (communist) party of Canada has approved Mr. Conn Smythe's proposal that the Toronto Maple Leafs play exhibition games in Russia. Is Mr. Smythe therefore to withdraw his offer, whatever its intrinsic merits? Of course not. On the second point, Korea Republic's attitude would leave little recourse except to settle international differences by violence. If recognition is to be withheld from Peiping because of disapproval of China's rulers, then how is business to be done with the Chinese nation? Negotiations could not for long be held, or bargains struck, or a settlement reached, if normal diplomatic intercourse is forever cut off. The South Korean regime is not universally approved in the
(Mr. Ellis.]
West, owing to President Syngman Rhee's endeavours to suppress opposition and establish a brutal police state. But his is the only government that exercises effective control over South Korea, and the West must recognize it. Much the same rule applies to China.
These are precisely the things we of the C.C.F. have been saying. The British government has said much the same thing, and has taken the same point of view. I believe that once and for all we should end these innuendoes and charges against people in this country who favour the recognition of the Peking government as though there was something insidious about it. I believe the record speaks for itself in that respect.
Along with the recognition of China there must, of course, go the question of China's entry into the United Nations. Much has been said by one or two hon. members about the possibility that China upon being recognized would become a member of the United Nations. The attitude some people have toward the United Nations is rather strange to say the least. Some people seem to believe that the United Nations is a sort of little social gathering in which all good people can be members, and all people we do not like can be kept out. In this regard I was very interested to read a report of a speech made by Sir Gladwyn Jebb in addressing the Pilgrims in London recently as reported in the Western Producer of March 25, under the heading "Jebb Urges Admission of Red China to U.N. Seat".
Sir Gladwyn Jebb, who was until recently the British representative at the UN, and who is now ambassador-designate to France, urged the United States to accept the principle of making the United Nations a true world forum in which peace can be won, and he warned:
"We are just not going to defeat communism by physical means, necessary though it may be to defend ourselves and the whole free world by such methods."
Another world war will not eliminate communism but will be more likely to extend it universally, perhaps under another name, he asserted.
Jebb commented that some Americans misconceive membership in the United Nations as a sort of prize for being a good boy, an attitude which he described as ignoring the world situation in which many governments "are not the sort of which we could possibly approve." "Somehow or other," he declared, "we have got to learn how to get on in this world with governments we dislike, and whose disappearance we should be the first to applaud if it could be accomplished by means other than war."
These are sentiments with which, I am certain, every member of the C.C.F. group would wholeheartedly agree.
The United Nations should be a true world forum. It is rather difficult to understand the nature of the criticism of the United

Nations from time to time. It is rather difficult to understand the point of view expressed by some members that you will weaken the United Nations by admitting the Peking government to membership when one realizes that if the United Nations is going to be a true world forum then all the major antagonists of the world should be brought together in order that the vital issues of the day may be discussed. Conversely, we have views such as those of the Social Credit group who would insist on the expulsion of the U.S.S.R. from the United Nations. Would that strengthen the United Nations? It depends entirely on what one's impression of the United Nations is.
If the United Nations is going to do the task for which it was created, apart from the work of the specialized agencies which of course are being carried on from day to day; if it is going to do a major job, then the United Nations is going to have to provide the machinery whereby the various antagonistic elements in the world may be brought together in order that common decisions may be arrived at. So far as the entry of China into the United Nations is concerned, the suggestion is made that it will double our difficulties and will increase obstructionist tactics. I would remind hon. members that I believe in every vote that has been taken in the general assembly of the United Nations the Russian bloc has usually been defeated by about eight to one, nine to one or ten to one. The veto power is already exercised by the Moscow government, and I think there would be very little change in that respect if the communist government of China also exercised that power.
But I do want to emphasize the point that we have got to clear the air with respect to what we consider the main job of the United Nations to be. We must realize, as Sir Gladwyn Jebb has pointed out, that we must make the United Nations a true world forum in which we will get all divergent points of view. There are some who say that we could get things done a lot better if the obstructionists were not there. I suppose some of the Liberals across the way might argue that too much time is spent on debate and that they would get the work of the house done much quicker if they got rid of the opposition. That is the same type of logic as to argue that the work of the United Nations would be facilitated by the expulsion of all those who might disagree with the majority decision. It is up to the majority to persuade the others.
Think of a United Nations in which you only have those who agree and all those who
External Affairs
disagree are expelled. It is like having a prize fight with only one boxer in the ring. It is difficult to conceive of the type of reasoning that would lead a person to advocate either the denial of entry of China to the United Nations or the expulsion of the U.S.S.R. from that body.
We are much concerned at the present moment with the coming Geneva conference. Something has been said about the apparent failure of the Berlin conference, but if the Berlin conference brought about the Geneva conference perhaps that is one positive accomplishment of that meeting. There are two attitudes of mind that may prevail among the delegates who go to Geneva. There may be those who will go with closed minds determined that under no circumstances will they yield on any point. Again, there are others who would be prepared to go to the conference and seek any area upon which some measure of agreement might be reached, no matter how small that area might be. I think we must realize that there are some who go to international conferences with closed minds.
I want to draw the attention of the house to a statement made recently by Representative Judd who is chairman of the House of Representatives foreign affairs subcommittee. His words are reported in an Associated Press dispatch from Washington which appeared in the Gazette of March 28. The report reads in part as follows:
Judd said any truce sought by the allies, rather than the communists, would be "the first step toward the war we are trying to avoid. If the communists come to us with evidence of good faith to negotiate, rather than with another trick or a trap, the United States is always willing to negotiate", he said. But Judd declared a genuine truce would be possible at Geneva only if "they (the communists) ceased being communists."
I think no comment is needed on that statement. It speaks for itself. The attitude of Canada at this conference is something that concerns us at the present moment. We have heard a number of speeches during the course of this debate by members who suggest almost the same kind of closed mind with respect to this conference. The statement was made: After all, what if they do promise to desist from further acts of aggression? We will not believe them anyway. Of course if we are going to take that attitude before the conference opens then we cannot blame anyone but ourselves if we find that no agreement at all comes out of the conference.
But there is one point in this connection that was dealt with very effectively by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Phil-pott). It is the matter of the red herring

External Affairs
involved in the use of the word "appeasement" and the reference to Munich in connection with present-day conferences. I find it difficult to understand how a student of world history who has taken the trouble to study the events leading up to the Munich conference and the events of the conference itself can possibly draw any parallel between Munich and conferences held under international auspices at the present time. The Munich conference was a conference to which were invited people who were virtually certain to agree on a particular course, and those who were likely to disagree were not invited. For example, Czechoslovakia, the country most concerned, simply was not invited to the conference because Czechoslovakia quite naturally would have taken great exception to the discussions that were going on at that time. Therefore I do not think anyone should seek at this time to use the Munich conference or the term "appeasement" as a red herring to try to throw difficulties in the way of those who would seek to bring about some small measure of understanding in the world today.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) dealt with an extremely important subject this afternoon. I am glad he did so because it absolves me from the necessity of saying some of the things I wished to say. I think it is an extremely important matter. If the new bomb is exploded next month we may be spared any disastrous consequences, but where is it going to end? Is there going to be further testing of still more powerful bombs? Where is the line going to be drawn? It has to be drawn somewhere, and I think we should give the most serious consideration to the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I do not wonder that he is concerned.
I noticed that last week the Vancouver Province published on its front page a map showing the danger area of a hydrogen bomb explosion such as the one to be exploded next month. The area on the map covered a radius of 450 miles. It extended almost as far north as Prince Rupert, and as far northeast as Edson, Alberta. It included the city of Calgary and the outskirts of Lethbridge and extended south to Missoula, Montana, and to an area just north of Grants Pass. It included the cities of Spokane, Seattle, Portland, Victoria and most of the settled areas of British Columbia. Is it any wonder that the hon. member, representing as he does a Pacific coast constituency, should have risen in his place this afternoon and have made the very valuable contribution he made to the debate? It is the enormous effects of such bombs that brought the Vancouver Province to publish an editorial on the matter. I just want to

draw your attention to this editorial because I think it sums up the situation in much the same terms as the Secretary of State for External Affairs used in his address just last Sunday to a group of young people in the city of Ottawa. In dealing with the threat of atomic war or the hydrogen bomb, the Vancouver Province of March 27, 1954 had this to say in part:
It can only be done by driving home the basic fact that no one will win an atomic war. The scattered, despairing fragments of the human race able to survive such a holocaust would not be very interested in the social theories of Karl Marx or anyone else.
The atom bomb has dwarfed all social theories. When and if the next atomic bomb is dropped as an act of war our ideologies, legal systems, ideas of government, learning, culture, will on that day be rendered mere bagsful of nonsense.
Nothing of value anywhere will survive an atomic war.
With this background, Mr. Speaker, I want to urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to see to it that the Canadian delegation at Geneva does everything within its power to seek at least small areas upon which there can be some degree of understanding and agreement. What is the alternative? The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of our movement, when speaking in this debate last Thursday pointed out the alternatives which face the world today. He stated the world had a choice of co-existence, if I may use that term, or we might seek to destroy them and they might seek to destroy us. Now, that is the choice before the world today, and I wonder where Canada will stand on this matter.
With this background in mind, I urge the government to take advantage of every possible opportunity to negotiate to come to even a slight degree of understanding on some of the issues that face the world today. Without such an understanding the world will continue to face the perpetual threat of destruction by a third world war.
