speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This debate that is now coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, and the conclusion of which will make it possible to set up the committee on external affairs where these and many other subjects might be discussed further, has ranged far and wide over the world. I do not believe any of us should complain about that because we have learned from the events of the last forty or fifty years that when international

relations break down our men have to range far and wide over the world, from Germany to Korea, in the defence of peace.
In the course of the discussion we have made excursions into the fields of history, philosophy, religion, and almost on occasion metaphysics. We have gone as far back as 8000 B.C. and spent a good deal of time looking at what is going to happen in April, 1954, at Geneva. During the course of the debate a great many questions have been raised, and a great deal of advice has been given to the government as to how to deal with them. As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said this afternoon, questions have been hurled at me. On the government's side, we should certainly do nothing but welcome that because advice is helpful, especially when it is good advice.
At times, however, some of the advice- this I suppose is inevitable-that has been given to us has been contradictory in character, especially on the subject of recognition of the Peking government in China. As I understand it from the speeches that have been given, the members of the Progressive Conservative party are afraid that we will recognize that government, and the members of the C.C.F. are worried that we will not. Naturally, therefore, the advice that has been given on that point has been slightly contradictory. I am not quite certain of the position of the official opposition in the matter, apart from the advice they have given as to what ours should be. I think in relation to recognition, and I will come back to this later, the position of the official opposition might be summed up in the words of a song, I think by Gilbert and Sullivan, "Never-well, hardly ever."
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and I think one or two other hon. members on the other side, suggested that we had been derelict in our responsibility on this side because neither the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) nor myself had said anything about the commonwealth of nations. I feel the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) dealt with that matter very effectively yesterday when he said that the Prime Minister had been giving evidence by deed and not only by word of his feeling for the commonwealth of nations which in its new form is very different from the old British Empire and has demonstrated once again the genius of the people composing it for political improvisation, if I may put it that way, and for service to the world.
The hon. member for Greenwood talked about the commonwealth of nations as a third centre of power and hoped that along that line its new usefulness might develop. With
External Affairs
all respect to him, I do not see the new commonwealth in that light, either politically or legally, because it is unrealistic, if I may use the word, to talk about a commonwealth composed of nations such as India on the one hand, South Africa on the other and the United Kingdom and the rest of us as a centre of power. There could be no single decision, as I see it, which would bring that power into action. It is not, therefore, a centre of power in the sense that the United States or the U.S.S.R. is. But it is a centre of cooperation and understanding. In that respect it is, and will continue I am sure, to render a very valuable service.
I hope that this centre of understanding and co-operation will not develop as a kind of third force-I have said this before- somewhere between the United States and the U.S.S.R. There are only two forces in the world today, or should be; those forces which are fighting for peace and good international relations and those that are on the opposite side of that issue.
I feel that I should say a few words right at the beginning about the speech made the other evening by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). He accused me softly last Friday of indulging in semantic subtleties. Well, there was nothing subtle about some of his statements. They were clear; but, as I see it, they were clearly wrong; they were directed as we remember for the most part to the United States and to the conduct of the western foreign ministers at Berlin. And I am not suggesting that the hon. member is anything like a fellow traveller, or a member of any fellow-travelling group when I criticize his stand on this matter.
He was pretty strong in his criticism of the western proposals at Berlin for the European defence community for the unification of Germany as obviously unacceptable to the Soviet union and, as he called it, the hasty western rejection of Mr. Molotov's proposals for European security.
What was wrong with these western proposals for the unification of Germany, based as they were upon the principle, which surely we must all accept, of free elections and the formation of a united German government which, once it was formed by free elections, would have full power to contract out of the European defence community if it desired to do so, if it happened to be in?
It seems to me to be most unfair, indeed absurd, to talk about a proposal of that kind, in contrast to the Soviet proposal on the same subject, as sabotaging the Berlin conference. In so far as Mr. Molotov's plan for European security was concerned, that was introduced

External Affairs
at the conference in Berlin on February 10. It was discussed by the foreign ministers at three meetings; and in spite of their efforts they failed to clarify some of its points, especially that of its relationship to NATO. Mr. Molotov refused to co-operate in that regard, but it became pretty clear before the conference ended that the acceptance of this scheme for European security would have meant the abandonment of NATO and its replacement, for European states, by a collective security system which would have included all of eastern European communist states, and the U.S.S.R. itself-which is more Asian than European-and would have excluded the United States and Canada and, indeed, the communist government in China. However that nation-and the U.S.A.-would have been permitted to attend the meetings of such a system as observers.
I think after the consideration which was given, and after their inability to get the clarification they desired, the western foreign ministers were entitled to claim that there was no basis for European peace or unity or security to be found in that particular proposal.
In a more general way the hon. member for Nanaimo stated his views, and I am quoting:
The western powers have been led to consort with all the most disreputable and reactionary elements in Europe to the destruction of the element in that society which might have built a better world in the heart of Europe.
Well, who are these "disreputable" elements? Are they the followers of Moscow, such as Togliatti, Duclos, Thorez, Field Marshal von Paulus, Grotewohl and Ulbricht? No, Mr. Speaker, they are, according to the hon. member, de Gasperi, Adenauer, Ernst Reuter, Robert Schuman, Georges Bidault or Jules Moch.
Later in his statement the hon. member criticized our policy at the United Nations, as he had every right to do. Then he ended up that phase of his remarks with these words:
We have left the other nations-
That is, Canada has done this.
-who are not nearly as well equipped as we are-
He did not specify any particular nation.

to stand up for principles of honesty and decency in the world.
And at another point he said:
I think on the most charitable basis we can only say that it has been a somewhat shabby role.
Well, I suggest that our participation in international affairs in recent years is not considered by most Canadians, or in fact by most countries, as justifying its characterization as a shabby role. We have of course

made mistakes, and I have no doubt we will continue to make some. But I hope we will never act in such a way that we can legitimately be charged with being shabby in respect of our international responsibilities.
And the hon. member ended up by saying that because of our deficiency in this regard many Canadians are slightly afraid and ashamed of being Canadians. Well, I will have to leave him to that company of Canadians who are slightly ashamed of being Canadians, and I do not think he will find too much companionship there.
Now, there has been a good deal of discussion in this debate about the European defence community, what it stands for and what our relationship to it should be. I did say in introducing this resolution that we supported the European defence community, and then I added the words "or something like it". The hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Eglinton both asked me what I meant by "or something like it". What are the alternatives?
Well, by "or something like it" I had in mind possibly some kind of amendment by protocol for consideration if the original agreement is not satisfactorily effected. And as for alternatives, I would suggest to the hon. member for Prince Albert that if he reads Hansard at page 1584, when I spoke on January 29, he will find that I outlined there the five possible alternatives to the existing international defence community now under consideration.
A good many members in the debate have expressed doubts and uneasiness about the acceptance and the putting into effect of the European defence community. I can understand that uneasiness, because I share it. And if we share it in this house we can certainly understand how citizens of countries close to Germany who have seen so much of invasion in recent years must feel about it. But while we may understand that feeling, still we must ask ourselves, as I have tried to ask myself: What is the alternative? While arguing the point of view that there must be something dangerous in the position, it would surely be wise to follow it up by suggesting a more satisfactory alternative. From my own study 1 do not think that there is a more satisfactory alternative, unless all those who are now discussing the present arrangement should get together and agree upon changes to it.
Appeals have been made to history in this connection. Well, I draw-and I am sure other hon. members also draw-other lessons from history which bear on the matter. I stated on January 29 that one method of

controlling German aggressive expansion is the old unhappy one, by which the west joined with the east against an independent armed Germany in central Europe. Neither in 1914 nor in 1939 was an alliance of that kind effective in preventing war, even if it may have been effective in winning war. And so, with the history of 1914 and 1939 very much in mind, plans for a European defence community have been drawn up in order to bring Germany into an alliance which would give scope for her energy and talents but which would also include safeguards against uncontrolled military expansion.
The EDC treaty, with which NATO would be associated, has provided safeguards which have already been explained in detail in this house. If we have not faith in those safeguards, then we have no reason to have faith in any other conditions imposed by human authority.
Nor do I think we have ground for faith in our ability to control Germany rearmament without this kind of collective organization. Nor do I think we should have much confidence, with the experience of the years between the wars and now, in our resolve, let alone our ability, to keep Germany neutral and disarmed. We have tried that before and it has worked for a few years, but the end result has certainly not made for peace. Therefore I do feel-and I repeat this feeling which I spoke about earlier and indeed as late as January 29-that the best of all alternatives now before us-indeed it is the only one officially now before us-is the European defence community.
The hon. member for Eglinton and one or two other hon. gentlemen have talked about the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the hon. member for Eglinton asked a specific question in this regard, whether, commenting on the press dispatch of an interview between the Prime Minister and General Gruenther in Paris, we had accepted recently any new commitments in regard to NATO forces. Notwithstanding any interpretation that might have been given to that particular press statement, which was inaccurate in this respect, we have not accepted any commitments in regard to NATO which have not already been made clear to the house.
The hon. member for Peace River brought up an important question in this regard when he wanted to know the effect, if any- and he was worried about this-of such an arrangement as that which has been entered into between Turkey and Pakistan on our commitments under NATO. It is true that Turkey and Pakistan have worked out a bilateral defence arrangement and I am sure
External Affairs
it will make its own contribution to peace and security in that area. But that does not add to our commitments merely because one of the two principals to that arrangement is a NATO member; because our obligation under NATO is to come to the help of, or at least to consider an attack on the metropolitan area of a member state as an attack on ourselves. Any action taken as a result of an outside agreement which brought one NATO country into action because of its obligation to another country that was not a member of NATO would not, as I understand it, involve our NATO commitment.
Then, in respect of NATO, there has been a good deal of talk about our ability to do more in implementing article 2. All I can say is that I realize that this has been a very slow and complicated and at times disappointing process. As I have already said before, in recent years we have subordinated the implementation of the non-defence aspects of NATO generally to the necessity for building up our defensive strength against a threat which seemed very dangerous at the time and remains dangerous. But we are doing something. Every time we meet at Paris we do something more to carry out the spirit of article 2, which is not concerned only with economic co-operation, but also with political co-operation generally; and in the meeting of the NATO council which will take place in a few weeks, on April 23, in Paris, as I think I said the other day, we have only one item on our agenda, namely, the exchange of views on the international political situation. That in itself, the fact that we can meet and talk about these things regularly, frankly and fully, does I think help to bring about this closer political integration, if I may use that word, which we had in mind when we signed the NATO agreement.
Having used the word "integration", I should refer to a question raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who asked for some clarification of the statement made by the Prime Minister at Bonn, which statement he felt went beyond anything that had previously been uttered in this house in regard to our international collective developments. On February 10, I think it was, at Bonn the Prime Minister said this:
It has become increasingly clear, I think, to all members of NATO and to those many countries who are associated with us throughout the free world that our very survival and our continued development in freedom and in peace depends upon our ability to look beyond national barriers and to make them somewhat less artificial and more satisfactory.

External Affairs
The Prime Minister added:
We believe the proper solution to the economic, cultural and spiritual betterment of all free peoples is to be found in an ever closer integration of their activities and in a greater sharing of their endeavours. More particularly, many of us believe the peoples living about the great basin of the Atlantic ocean might well seek the solution to their problem of economic betterment, political stability and self-defence in this closer integration of their national resources and of their machinery of government.
The Prime Minister of course had in mind when he made that statement-and I think it is one to which none of us would want to take exception-that the hope of the world today, especially the hope of the Atlantic world, and especially under the circumstances of today, must lie mainly in closer and closer co-operation and closer and closer relationship between governments and the agencies of government. In saying that he did not, I suggest, go so far as-certainly not any farther than-Mr. Mackenzie King did in this house on December 17, 1945, when he said-and these words might well be remembered by the hon. gentleman:
The more deeply one ponders the problems with which our world is confronted, in the light-"the terrible light," as Mr. Attlee said-of the implications of the development of atomic energy,-
I do not know what he would have said if he had been speaking today. I continue: -the harder it is to see a solution in anything short of some surrender of national sovereignty.
Mr. King went on:
With a limited surrender of national sovereignty, there must be instituted some form of world government restricted, at least at the outset, to matters pertaining to the prevention of war, and the maintenance of international security.
I think the lesson of the events of the last two or three days drives home that feeling that there is no safety for us, there is no security for us except in closer and closer international co-operation and more effective international arrangements to protect national security. And in bringing this about-this had been said in other parliaments than ours -there must be some relinquishment of national sovereignty, because the world is too small for jealous competing sovereignties in the circumstances of today. This, as a matter of fact, is not in one sense giving up national sovereignty at all. It consists, as Mr. Wendell Willkie used to say, of making national sovereignty work for us in the interests of national security.
A good many questions were asked about atomic energy matters. The hon. member for Prince Albert asked whether we had any international obligations at the present time with regard to extending present knowledge of atomic energy along the lines of making industry a partner of this development. The

answer to that question is no, we have not. He also asked questions relating to the proposed international agency which I had mentioned in my earlier statement. In fact he repeated to me some of the questions I had myself asked in that statement. At this stage I regret that I cannot do more than refer to the proposals themselves made by President Eisenhower when he pointed out that it was expected-and we share this expectation-that the proposed international agency, which is now under discussion, would be set up under the aegis of the United Nations. He also proposed that the governments principally involved-and that would include Canada-should, to the extent permitted by elementary prudence, make contributions from their stockpiles of normal uranium and fissionable materials to the international agency, and he added that ratio of contributions, procedures and other details would properly be within the scope of private conversations. Those private conversations are now going on.
It seems to me that at this stage it would be unwise for any of us to make public statements as to what we think can best be done to implement this general proposal. We have been in close touch with the United Kingdom government as well as the United States government on this matter. The United States government indeed is acting at the present time, as I said the other day, bilaterally with the U.S.S.R. and has put certain proposals to the government in Moscow. Those proposals have not been made public. They go into this matter in somewhat more detail than I have been able to do; but until we get the first reaction of Moscow to those proposals I think it would be unwise and indeed inappropriate for me to say anything more about the details of this matter than I have already said.
I appreciate, as must all hon. members, the uneasiness which has been reflected in this house over recent atomic developments. Yet I cannot help adding that I would be far more worried if those awful explorations into the science and the chemistry of destruction were exclusively in the hands of those whom we have cause to fear rather than in the hands of those who we know will not use them for any aggressive warlike purpose. Having said that, however, we cannot refrain from asking ourselves this question: Where are we going in this matter? As reported at page 3342 of Hansard, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government should make immediate representations to the United States, urging the United States not to undertake these experiments in the Pacific ocean.

As I indicated, I think it was yesterday, in the house, we have been in touch with United States authorities about the results of the recent explosion and have endeavoured to obtain information about the plans for subsequent explosions. We know-and our information in the last few days reinforces our knowledge-that those who have a special responsibility in this matter on our side in Washington share the anxiety of all people of good will at the horrible potentialities of the forces now being developed, and they are as anxious as we are to remove those anxieties. At this moment I can only repeat, as expressing my own feelings, what Sir Winston Churchill said yesterday in the House of Commons in London:
... I am sure that those responsible for conducting these tests will continue to take the most rigorous precautions to minimize the risks involved.
Our interest in this matter has already been expressed in Washington, as no doubt has the interest of other governments, and quite understandably so. But the best way to remove dangers in this field, as in other fields, and the best way to prevent any possible use of those weapons, is to prevent war. I do not desire to use language which is too shrill or excitable, but I cannot help feeling -as other hon. members have felt and have so expressed themselves-almost horror at the magnitude of the destructive forces now being made available for human use. When we talk about things like this it is customary to say that we must reduce the particular subject to its proper perspective. However far you reduce this matter to perspective, the perspective remains horrible.
I would go further, and this is as far as I can go at this time in answer to the impassioned and sincere appeal of my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East. I would agree that all governments concerned-and that includes the Canadian government- should, if I may use the expression, take a new look at United Nations international efforts in this field of the prevention of the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes. The clouds that have arisen eighteen or nineteen miles above that Pacific atoll; the deep and jagged cave that was blown into the bed of the Pacific ocean; and the men who, miles away, suffered merely by contact with the effects of the explosion; all these things surely impose on all of us, and no doubt especially on those of us who have some official responsibility, the obligation to take some kind of action, if one can find it, to harness these forces for constructive ends.
I agree that, in the light of what has happened, we must approach this problem- all of us; all governments-with a greater sense of urgency than possibly we have been 83276-224
External Affairs
showing in recent months. That requires, of course, action at the United Nations or at least international action. It may mean that we should re-examine our own attitude towards the question of international ownership of fissionable material as essential to a solution. But it also emphasizes the desirability, indeed the necessity, of bringing about some form of genuine international control and international inspection, without which anxieties in this matter will not be removed.
I now pass on to some other subjects which have arisen in the course of the debate and move from this question of atomic energy to the Pacific. More than one speaker in this debate has suggested that it should be the aim of our policy in the free world to do everything possible to separate the communist satellites from the U.S.S.R. The leader of the official opposition, speaking on Yugoslavia, said, as reported on page 3377 of Hansard:
... it is my hope that under the influence of the outside world Yugoslavia may gradually emerge from communism into a better form of government that will bring freedom to its people.
Then he added that this is only possible once the people are separated from Moscow.
I think we can all agree with that statement in principle, but it is not always so easy to find the proper policy to encourage that separation. Right Hon. Anthony Eden, in the article which my hon. friend quoted from the Daily Telegraph of London, dated January 20, 1950, said as follows:
Independent nationalist communism (in China) is certainly possible later-but we should be unwise to count on it.
I agree with that statement and I agree further that we should be unwise to base our policy on its happening. Nevertheless, we should take advantage of any opportunity that may present itself to bring that sort of thing about. One such opportunity has been put forward in some quarters as existing at this time, in increasing importance, namely in encouraging and developing trade between the east and the west. The other night, as reported at page 3380 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition said this:
. . . we do not need to sell our principles for a few dollars' worth of trade.
That is right, Mr. Speaker, we do not need to do that; and so far as this government is concerned, I am sure we do not intend to do so. It is true, however, that there are efforts now being made by the U.S.S.R. and communist governments to increase such trade. Why such efforts are being made at this time must of course be a matter for speculation, but one can be sure they contain much political and propaganda

External Affairs
content. I believe we can also be pretty sure that these efforts are not designed to help us. But it is still not impossible that some countries of the free world would be assisted by an increase in east-west trade, that their economic strength would be made greater by that trade, and that that in turn - would strengthen their defensive capacity.
The President of the United States himself as recently as yesterday, in his message to congress, had something to say about this. He said:
Curtailment of our aid programs will increase the pressures for resumption of such trade. A greater exchange of peaceful goods between east and west so far as it can be achieved without jeopardizing national security, and subject to our embargo on communist China and North Korea, should not cause us undue concern.
So far as trade in strategic goods is concerned, no question arises because that is prohibited, and that prohibition will remain as long as circumstances remain as they are at present. But we should do our best to agree as to what is to be included on that list. So far as the proposals for trade in non-strategic goods are concerned, I suggest that each one of these can be considered on its merit, and that consideration will have to include, of course, our experiences in the past, to which allusion was made the other evening, and in regard to the risk of relying on such trade, and the fact that we should not deceive ourselves that we are likely to find in the Soviet union, for example, any considerable market at any time for Canadian agricultural products.
It is true that Soviet agricultural policy has, if not collapsed, at least been very disappointing to those who have been responsible for it, and it is true, according to our information, that there are shortages of agricultural products in the U.S.S.R. But I would remind the house that in the twenties, at a time when there was famine in Russia, the Soviet union of that day did not hesitate to export agricultural products to obtain the currency which they needed for their own industrialization. I believe we would be making an optimistic mistake if we expected the Soviet union to be a lucrative market for Canadian exports of that kind.
There is a paragraph, Mr. Speaker, from the Randall report which was submitted to congress the other day on the question of east-west trade, which I think is worth reading. That report contains this paragraph:
It may well be, moreover, that more trade in goods for peaceful purposes would in itself serve to penetrate the iron curtain and advance the day when normal relationships with the peoples of eastern Europe may be resumed.

Sir Winston Churchill on February 25 last put this idea in somewhat more positive and indeed more optimistic terms when he said in London:
The more the two great divisions of the world mingle in healthy and fertile activities of commerce, the greater is the counterpoise to purely military calculations. Other thoughts take up their place in the minds of men. Friendly infiltration can do nothing but good. We have no reason to fear it, and if communist Russia does not fear it, that in itself is a good sign.
I do not know if our optimism would go as far as that, but I think we will all agree that this problem of trade with the U.S.S.R. is a complex one except in so far as trade in strategic goods is concerned; and that proposals to this end should be considered by the government from the point of view of our own national interest which, in the case of the countries of the free world coalition, cannot be divorced from the collective interests of us all.
There were some other questions on Asia and the Pacific raised in the course of this debate. It was pointed out by more than one speaker that we should do what we can as a government and as a country to prevent or assist in the prevention of further aggressive communist conquests in that part of the world.
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked me whether we would support the speech made in New York the night before last by the United States Secretary of State in respect of Indo-China. The hon. member quoted from that speech and I will put that quotation on the record a little more. On that occasion Mr. Dulles said:
Under all the circumstances it seems desirable to clarify further the United States position.
Under the conditions today, the imposition on southeast Asia of the political system of communist Russia and its Chinese communist ally, by whatever means, would be a grave threat to the whole free community. The United States feels that that possibility should not be passively accepted, but should be met by united action. This might involve serious risks. But these risks are far less than those that will face us a few years from now, if we dare not be resolute today.
That, of course, is a very important statement. As a government and as a parliament we should study it and find out what is involved in it before we are asked to commit ourselves either to unreserved support, or indeed to criticism of it. But I suggest this is not the time when we should be asked to line up behind it, ahead of it or against it, especially until we find out what is meant by the very important words "united action". We are, of course, taking steps to secure an analysis and explanation of what was meant by that particular statement.

I am sure we all agree there is a real danger in the extension at the present time of communist aggression in Indo-China.
There is also a danger of not supporting the existing Asian democracies as an obstacle to the extension of communism in Asia, about which so many fears have rightly been expressed. I believe that the basis of Asian security today is not only collective action against communist aggression of the kind that has been indicated, but the strengthening of Asian democracies and giving them all the support we possibly can.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra in his speech yesterday once again brought to my attention the importance of Pacific security arrangements and the necessity for Canada participating in collective security arrangements in that region. The hon. member complained that I had pooh-poohed the importance of this matter in the past and did not seem to take it very seriously. I would like to refresh his memory for a moment, Mr. Speaker, by recalling debates we have had in this house on this very matter, and especially last February when I went with great detail into the reasons why at this time Canada's accession to membership in any of these Pacific security arrangements was not practical.
Since the last statement I made on this subject the ANZUS council has had another meeting, of which my hon. friend is no doubt aware, in Washington on the 9th and 10th of September last year, and the communique issued at the end of that council meeting included the following statement:
The council-
That is the ANZUS council.
-affirmed its readiness to consider any measure which would strengthen the defence of the area.
83276-224J
External Affairs
The Pacific area.
It unanimously-
That includes Australia and New Zealand.
-concluded, however, that to attempt to enlarge its membership would not contribute directly and materially to this end.
Soon after the council concluded its meeting Mr. Dulles had the following to say by way of comment on this point:
It is, however, unlikely that any one of these existing treaties-
The Pacific treaties.
-could itself be the framework for such development.
That is, a general security pact in the Pacific.
Indeed, before there can be much useful development by way of multilateral treaties there is need for the development, within the Pacific area, of a greater measure of international good will and a greater unity of purpose.
I suggest that the hon. member is not fair to the government when he suggests that we show no interest in this matter or are defaulting on our obligations to participate in collective security arrangements in the Pacific. Surely we have given evidence more than once of our interest in Pacific security which, as a matter of fact, is not separable from Atlantic security. But for us to try to barge our way into the ANZUS arrangement or any other Pacific security arrangement at this time would not be very good diplomacy in the face of the information that has been conveyed to us and, indeed, in the face of the efforts of the United Kingdom, whose efforts to join this organization have not been very successful. In that regard I might point out that United Kingdom interest in this matter is at least as great as ours because it has Asian and Pacific territory. Therefore I commend to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra this extract from Sir Winston Churchill's statement in the House of Commons yesterday when he was being pressed to make representations to the United States on another matter which he did not think would be successful:
Blunt refusals are very serious things. We do not in diplomacy, and even in relations with the most friendly and kindred allies, lead up to anything that may finish in a blunt refusal.
I hope my hon. friend will take my assurance that if we have any reason to believe that we would get anything but a blunt refusal in the expression of our interest in further Pacific security arrangements we would be glad to investigate the matter further.

External Affairs

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Has he explored the possibility of Canada becoming a party to the ANZUS treaty?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, we have, in Washington, as to the views of the United States government, and in Australia, as to the views of the Australian government, concerning the extension of the ANZUS treaty to include other states. I should think the statements I have just put on the record from the communique of the council and from Mr. Dulles would give the hon. member a clear-cut answer to any such explorations.

speechtext: Has the minister any alternative type of agreement to suggest?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, we are in continuous consultation with our friends in Washington and other places on this matter. The hon. member mentioned yesterday that Senator Knowland had recently proposed further discussions with respect to the broadening of these security arrangements. We were interested in that, and if the United States administration felt that would be a useful and wise thing to do at this time and we were invited, together with other countries, to participate in any discussions which were designed to bring about greater security in the Pacific, naturally we would give any such invitation the most sympathetic consideration. I cannot go any further than that now, nor do I think I should be asked to do so.
I come now to a subject that, while not the most important, has been the one raised most often in this debate, the question of the recognition of the communist government in China. I should like to say a few words on that subject to clear up the position of the government, if it needs clearing. Legal recognition is, as has already been pointed out in this debate, something you give for your own national advantage in your own national interest, which includes as the most important objective of all, maintaining and strengthening the peace. If, as has been pointed out this afternoon, recognition meant giving approval, if it were only a question of moral judgment, we should today, I suggest, have no diplomatic contact with communist countries-except the communist country of Yugoslavia which is in a very different category- in our own capital or at the United Nations. On this point of recognition Mr. Dulles, speaking the day before yesterday in New York, said:
Generally, it Is useful that there should be diplomatic intercourse between those who exercise de facto governmental authority and it is well established that recognition does not imply moral approval.

"Does not imply moral approval", he said. He went on:
President Monroe, in his famous message to congress, denounced the expansionist and despotic system of czarist Russia and its allies. But he said that it would nevertheless be our policy "to consider the government de facto as the legitimate government for us." That has indeed been the general United States policy, and I believe that it is a sound general policy. However, where it does not serve our interests we are free to vary from it.
The Leader of the Opposition, speaking the other day on this point, said that recognition also means admission to the United Nations. Here is what he said:
Do not let the Secretary of State for External Affairs or anyone else in the house suggest it can be otherwise.
Yet that is exactly what the hon. gentleman himself suggested on January 29, as found at page 1621 of Hansard. He said:
Let us remember, of course, the distinction between recognition and entry into the United Nations. There seems to be confusion about that. Recognition simply means formal recognition of a government as the de facto government of the state with which we are prepared to do business. Whether or not we are prepared to do business with communist China is something still to be considered, but there is a vast difference between recognition and the entry of the government of communist China into the United Nations.
I suggest that the hon. gentleman was right on at least one of those occasions. But I do not think it matters very much whether or not it means entry into the United Nations. It is more of an academic question than otherwise at the moment. There are a good many members of the United Nations today who have recognized communist China and have not voted for her admission into the United Nations when that subject has come up. There are other states which have been recognized by practically every government in the world and are not members of the United Nations.
The Leader of the Opposition also said that he was "against recognition under present conditions and in the circumstances of today." That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly the position of the government and I think it explains what I meant when I said in Chicago that we were a little more careful in our attitude and, as I thought, more realistic than they were over there. We do not say, as has been said elsewhere, that we will "never" recognize the government now in authority in China. We have said that if conditions and circumstances change we will have another look at the matter. Surely that is only common sense. For as the Leader of the Opposition said, as found at page 3381 of Hansard:
No one can say that anything is forever in this very uncertain world.

But then the Leader of the Opposition added that in my statement reported from Windsor I went further than that, and I suggest that I did not. He quoted the words attributed to me in a Canadian Press dispatch, and I am not quarrelling with its accuracy a bit. These were the words:
If Red China adopts a conciliatory attitude at the Geneva conference, Canada might take a new look at this problem.
Then, I added, "Remember that conference is to be about Korea."
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) then referred to what a reporter in Windsor called a summary of further observations and from this summary he built up the thesis that we were contemplating some kind of early recognition or some kind of deal at Geneva -I use that word not in any unparliamentary sense-which might bring about recognition. This summary, the words of which the Leader of the Opposition, as reported on page 3374 of Hansard for March 26, 1954, were mistakenly attributed to me-and I know that was accidental-reports me as having said:
If the Reds are willing to give assurances that their aggression in Korea is a thing of the past and that they are ready to take an honest line in international affairs, he said, Canada must consider following Great Britain's lead in recognizing the Peking regime.
Well that summary, as summaries often do, gave a wrong impression if interpreted to mean that all the Peking government has to do at Geneva is to say, "We are sorry; we will be a respectable government in the future", and then we will recognize them. My own recollection, based on the notes I had, gives a somewhat different picture than the summary. I believe, however, that one indication of changed circumstances which would bring about, as I see it, another look by the government at this matter, would be an assurance, not merely by words, that the Chinese communist forces were willing to withdraw from Korea and agree to a peace settlement in Korea in accordance with the principles laid down by the United Nations. The end of aggression in Indo-China would be another such indication.
The Leader of the Opposition was very sceptical, and I am not quarrelling with him on this, about the value of any assurances from communists. After some experience in the matter I am inclined to agree that verbal or written assurances from that quarter are very often worthless. But, Mr. Speaker, I had in mind the kind of assurance that the member for Prince Albert was no doubt talking about when he gave the government this
External Affairs
advice in referring to the Geneva conference. I am quoting from page 3340 of Hansard for March 25, 1954:
I think Canadians will expect that the minister at the Geneva conference . . . will demand the fullest assurances that aggression will be banished by it.
It is that kind of assurance that might make it possible for us to have a new look at this question.
Meanwhile the fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we are going to deal with and to negotiate with this Chinese government at Geneva at a political conference. In doing so we are merely recognizing the facts of the present situation. Mr. Eden was quoted by the Leader of the Opposition the other day as saying that the decision to recognize communist China is eventually inescapable. I will not go as far as that. I do not know. But the necessity of dealing at Geneva with this government is certainly inescapable. That is the reason we are going to Geneva.
The other night the Leader of the Opposition suggested that British policy on the recognition of communist China was that of the Labour government and not necessarily that of the United Kingdom as a whole. He felt that some statements of Mr. Eden's supported that point of view. I suggest that that is not a historically accurate portrayal of the situation because the leader of the Conservative party, shortly before recognition was given on November 17, 1950-Mr. Churchill, as he then was-said that diplomatic relations should be established with the communist regime. The Conservative party, as a party, did not oppose the Labour government of the day in London when it announced its decision.
So far as Canada is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we will not act at Geneva, I hope, in a way which would betray national honour, national interests, or our hopes for peace. We are going there, so far as Korea is concerned, to convert an armistice into a peace. We have a United Nations resolution for that purpose which, as I suggested the other day, will be our instructions on this matter.
It has been said by more than one hon. member of the opposition that we have adopted a different attitude in respect to Indo-China. We were asked why we did not show a more active interest in the IndoChinese problem, which is possibly as important to the peace of the world as the Korean problem. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is a very real difference between the two positions in so far as Canadian participation.

External Affairs
if not Canadian interests, is concerned. We have been invited to Geneva, as a member of the United Nations with forces participating in Korea, to help bring about a peace settlement. The text of the invitation makes that quite clear, and I shall read it: In accordance with the proposal agreed upon at a meeting of the foreign ministers of the United States, France, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union, February 18, 1954, and announced in the enclosed communique of the same date the government of the United States has the honour to extend to the government of Canada an invitation to participate, if it so desires, in the Korean political conference to be convened at Geneva on April 26.
In so far as the Indo-Chinese aspect of this conference is concerned, the communique of the foreign ministers in Berlin has this to say. They are agreeable that the problem of restoring peace in Indo-China will also be discussed at the conference, to which representatives of the United States, France, United Kingdom, Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Chinese People's Republic and other interested states will be invited. Our position here is, however, entirely different. We have not been invited to take part in the Indo-Chinese discussions. There was a basis for our invitation to the Korean peace conference because we are a participating power in the Korean operation. It might be a quite different situation in so far as Indo-China is concerned.
It may well be that those most immediately concerned will want to keep that conference restricted to those who are actually concerned with Indo-Chinese operations.

speechtext: Would the minister be kind enough to read that communique again, because it does not seem to be capable of the interpretation he is putting upon it.

speechtext: It says they are agreed that the problem in Indo-China will also be discussed at the conference-that is the Korean conference-to which representatives-that is to the Indo-Chinese discussion-to which representatives of the United States, France, United Kingdom, Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Chinese People's Republic and other interested states will be invited.

speechtext: That surely refers to the Korean conference.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has been made quite clear to us that "the interested parties" refers to those who may be invited to the IndoChinese talks. If we are invited we shall play as active a part as we can. However, if it appears to be in the best interests of settling the problem that the discussion be restricted to the four or five countries

immediately concerned, I do not think it would serve the best interests of peace to press for an invitation.
In the process of negotiations at Geneva, concessions of some kind may be necessary on both sides to reach any solution. For instance, if some concessions had not been made and some compromise had not been reached at Panmunjom-a compromise upon which the United Nations did not desert its principles-we would have had no armistice at all and no peace negotiations could even be attempted in Geneva. No one I assume opposes or opposed at the time the armistice, and no one in this house opposes the invitation to the Geneva conference. It may be that the hon. member for Prince Albert has some mental reservation about the wisdom of this conference. He is quoted as having said in Toronto, according to the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 9, that the Red Chinese attendance at the conference in Geneva is a victory for Russia. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the case; because China will not be in Geneva as one of the five great powers, or after recognition, or even as an inviting power. Indeed, it is hard to imagine Mr. Dulles, Mr. Eden or Mr. Bidault agreeing to a proposal for a conference at Geneva, if it were a victory for Russia.
Red China will be at that conference in Geneva because we cannot negotiate a peace in Korea without her attendance. Whether we can do it with her attendance remains to be seen.
On February 2, 1951, I said in the house, referring to the Chinese communists:
They should not think that they can bludgeon or blackmail their way into recognition or the United Nations.
I still feel that way, and also feel that Peking should not be granted diplomatic recognition merely because they signed an armistice in Korea or have agreed to go to a conference in Geneva. But that does not mean that we will not negotiate with this government now in authority in China, when we should do so, or with any other communist government when it is necessary to do so.
We have accepted this invitation, and I hope the Canadian delegation will not follow any course at Geneva or take any action there which would justify the gloomy forebodings expressed last Friday by the Leader of the Opposition, based upon impressions-and as I see it erroneous impressions-that he had received from press quotations. We are not carrying an umbrella to Geneva, nor are we brandishing a bomb either.
Last Friday some pretty violent language was used in respect of some who will be

attending this conference. Communist leaders were called thieves and murderers, and there was talk about compromising with the devil. There was talk about the extermination of these tormentors and betrayers of humanity.
I am not sure that very much is gained by this kind of talk on the eve of a meeting, the invitation to which we have accepted and which, after all, cannot achieve anything positive except by some kind of agreement after negotiation with these people.
Then, having painted a pretty black picture of what we are up against, the leader of the official opposition surprised me by saying also-
